title: The Cave and the Carob: Rashbi, the Thirteen Years, and the Book Written in His Name
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Gush Halav, the house of Yochai
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no source names his birthplace and none dates his birth; the year is a modern back-calculation from his years under Akiva
stops.campa: The olive town of Gush Halav stands on the north-eastern slope of Mount Meron, thirteen kilometres above Safed, and tradition puts the household of Yochai here. No Talmudic source names the place, and none names a year. The town is remembered as his because his son Elazar will one day be buried in its ground, and because the Galilee keeps its own account of who belonged to it. The law he is taught is the law of a sacrificial religion with no altar left to perform it on. He is born under garrison, among olive presses and terraces, twenty years after the Temple burned.
suggested_refs: The olive terraces and ruined synagogue of Gush Halav (Jish), Upper Galilee
sources: Pesikta de-Rav Kahana, on Elazar's burial at Gush Halav

stops.name: Yavne, the academy on the coastal plain
stops.date_confidence: attested by Berakhot 28a, which Zecharias Frankel judged chronologically spurious; the placement stands or falls with that passage
stops.campa: The academy Rabban Gamliel II rebuilt after the Temple fell sits near the sea, in a town that smells of salt and of ink, and the young man from the Galilee sits in it among sages reconstituting an entire law out of a ruin. Berakhot 28a preserves an exchange from these years, with Gamliel and Joshua ben Hananiah present. It is also the passage Zecharias Frankel called spurious: about forty-five years after this scene, when Akiva was thrown into prison, Shimon's father was still living. The arithmetic will not close.
suggested_refs: Zecharias Frankel, Darkhei ha-Mishnah (Leipzig, 1859), where the Yavne placement is rejected

stops.name: Bnei Brak, thirteen years in Akiva's house of study
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Leviticus Rabbah 21 gives the thirteen years without fixing them in a calendar
stops.campa: For thirteen years he sits in Rabbi Akiva's study house, inside the circle admitted to the deepest layers of the master's teaching. Leviticus Rabbah supplies the number. Who sat beside him through it is not agreed. Encyclopaedia Judaica names Hanina ben Hakhinai; the Jewish Encyclopedia pairs him instead with Rabbi Meir; Yevamot 62b gives a third arrangement again, five students taught in the south after twenty-four thousand disciples died in a single season. Shimon appears in all three lists. Which man actually sat next to him for thirteen years is a question none of the sources answers.
suggested_refs: The study house of Akiva at Bnei Brak, remembered in Leviticus Rabbah 21
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Simeon bar Yohai', via Encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the death of Akiva
stops.date_confidence: attested as an execution scene; whether Shimon was present is nowhere stated
stops.campa: In the provincial capital the governor has Akiva's flesh raked with iron combs. The revolt is broken, Hadrian's decrees stand over the province, and the teachers of Torah are being killed as a class. Later tradition holds that students of Akiva saw the death or its aftermath and carried it into their own defiance of Rome; whether Shimon stood in that crowd, no source says. The old man recites the Shema through the combs and draws the word echad, one, out to the length of his breath, and dies on it.
suggested_refs: The Roman theatre and praetorium of Caesarea Maritima, seat of the governor
sources: adriano.journey.json, on the Hadrianic decrees and the Bar Kokhba revolt

stops.name: Between Usha and Shefaram, the ordination in the pass
stops.date_confidence: attested: Sanhedrin 14a places the act in open country between two towns
stops.campa: Ordination has been made a capital crime, for the man ordained and for the town that harbours the act. Judah ben Bava takes five students into the open country between Usha and Shefaram, outside any settlement, so that no place can be punished for what he is about to do, and he ordains them there. Roman soldiers find him. He tells the five to run, and they run; the soldiers drive three hundred iron spears through him and leave him like a sieve. Shimon bar Yochai is one of the five who got away.
suggested_refs: The pass between Usha and Shefaram, Lower Galilee

stops.name: Usha, the word about the roads
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Shabbat 33b names no town for this conversation, and the setting at Usha is a later inference
stops.campa: Three sages are sitting, and Yehuda ben Gerim is sitting beside them. Rabbi Yehuda opens: how pleasant are the works of this nation, the marketplaces, the bathhouses, the bridges. Rabbi Yose says nothing at all. Shimon answers that everything they made, they made for themselves, marketplaces for harlots, bathhouses for their own bodies, bridges to take the toll. Yehuda ben Gerim repeats the conversation and it reaches the government. Yehuda who praised is elevated, Yose who was silent is exiled to Sepphoris, and Shimon is sentenced to death.
suggested_refs: The reconstituted Sanhedrin at Usha, to which the scene is traditionally assigned

stops.name: A study hall in the Galilee, the wife's daily walk
stops.date_confidence: attested event, unlocated: the source names no town and no room
stops.campa: Father and son hide first in a house of study, and his wife walks to them each day with a loaf of bread and a cup of water. When the search tightens he says what the danger has made him think: the authorities will press her, she will not be able to hold out, and both of them will be taken. So they leave the one roof they know for open country. The Talmud names no town for the house and no room inside it, only the loaf, the cup, and the walk she made every day until they went.
suggested_refs: The unnamed beit midrash of Shabbat 33b, first refuge of the flight

stops.name: The cave above Peki'in, the carob and the spring
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Shabbat 33b names no place for the cave; Peki'in is later Galilean tradition, Gadara the reading of the older biographical accounts
stops.campa: They go and they hide in a cave. The text says nothing more about where, and two later traditions fill the silence differently: the older biographical accounts put the cave near Gadara, while the Galilee itself puts it in the hill above Peki'in, where there is a mouth in the rock to point at. At the entrance a carob tree and a spring of water are created for them. Nothing else comes in from outside. They eat from the tree and drink from the spring.
stops.quote: A miracle occurred and a carob tree was created for them as well as a spring of water.
suggested_refs: The cave shown above Peki'in, and the carob standing beside it
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Simeon ben Yohai' (the Gadara reading)

stops.name: The cave, buried to the neck in sand
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the years in the cave are counted in the source, not dated
stops.campa: They own one set of clothes between them and it will have to last. So they strip, and sit in sand up to their necks, and study Torah all day out of the ground; at the hours of prayer they climb out, dress, pray, undress, and bury themselves again. Sand works at skin for twelve years. Sores open over both of them and stay open. Neither man says anything about them; the cloth is what is being protected, and the cloth comes through the twelve years intact while the two bodies inside it do not.
stops.quote: They sat in the cave for twelve years.
suggested_refs: The sand floor of the cave, the detail Shabbat 33b insists on

stops.name: The desert near Lod, the cave the Zohar puts him in
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a Zoharic tradition contradicting the Galilean one; the pin marks the town of Lod only, since no cave has ever been named
stops.campa: A rival strand of the story, carried in Zoharic material rather than in the Talmud, moves the thirteen years south, to a cave in the desert near Lod, closer to the coastal plain and its garrisons. The two geographies do not reconcile and no source has attempted to reconcile them. Nobody has proposed a specific cave here, no itinerary has brought pilgrims to one, and the tradition survives as one sentence contradicting another. The Galilee kept the northern cave and shows it. Which of the two readings came first is a question nobody has been able to settle.
suggested_refs: The Zoharic desert-cave tradition, unlocated and unexcavated

stops.name: The cave, Elijah at the entrance
stops.date_confidence: traditional: twelve years counted from a flight that is itself undated
stops.campa: Elijah the Prophet comes and stands at the mouth of the cave and speaks, not to them but into the air, the way news is delivered to men who cannot be addressed directly: who will inform bar Yochai that the emperor has died and his decree is annulled. Which emperor is never said. Later harmonizers offer Hadrian, dead in 138, or Antoninus Pius, dead in 161, and the arithmetic has never come out for either one. Father and son hear it and climb into the daylight of the twelfth year.
stops.quote: Who will inform bar Yohai that the emperor died and his decree has been abrogated?
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 33b, as standardly rendered (William Davidson Edition); this line was not verified verbatim against the source text during research
suggested_refs: The unresolved chronology of Hadrian, d. 138, against Antoninus Pius, d. 161
sources: Wikipedia, 'Shimon bar Yochai', on the unresolved identity of the emperor

stops.name: The fields below the cave, what the eyes do
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: They come down into the ordinary world and it is plowing season. Men are in the fields turning soil and dropping seed, doing the thing that must be done if anyone is to eat next year. He looks at them and says they have abandoned eternal life for temporal life, and everywhere his eyes fall the ground catches fire. Then a voice comes out of heaven and asks whether they emerged in order to destroy the world, and orders them back. They turn around and go back in.
stops.quote: These people abandon eternal life of Torah study and engage in temporal life for their own sustenance.
suggested_refs: The bat kol of Shabbat 33b, the second voice at the cave

stops.name: The cave, the thirteenth year
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Twelve months more in the rock, and the text gives the measure without apology: the judgment of Gehenna is twelve months, so twelve months is what is imposed. What twelve years made, the thirteenth is meant to unmake. Nothing is recorded of what the two of them said to each other down there the second time, or whether the carob went on fruiting, or whether they went back into the sand. The source keeps the count and nothing else: twelve years, then one more.
suggested_refs: The thirteenth year, counted separately in Shabbat 33b

stops.name: The road at dusk, the old man with two bundles of myrtle
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: It is Friday, near dark, and an old man goes past them at a run holding two bundles of myrtle. What are these for. For the honour of the Sabbath. Why two. One for remember, one for observe, the two verbs the fourth commandment carries, which the tradition says were spoken as a single word at Sinai by a mouth no human throat can manage. Elazar's eyes are still burning; his father's have stopped. Shimon turns to his son and says: see how precious the commandments are to Israel.
suggested_refs: The two bundles of myrtle, remember and observe, of Shabbat 33b

stops.name: Hamat Tiberias, the springs and the son-in-law
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event; the Talmud names only the bathhouse, and Hamat Tiberias is a traditional identification
stops.campa: Down out of the hills to the lake shore. Pinchas ben Yair, his son-in-law by the Talmud's own word, takes him to the hot water and bathes him, and when he sees what thirteen years of sand have done to the man's skin he begins to weep, and the tears fall into the cracks and burn. Woe to me that I have seen you like this, he says. The springs south of Tiberias have run sulphurous and hot since before the Romans came, and are running still. Shimon answers him out of the water.
stops.quote: Happy are you that you have seen me like this, as had you not seen me like this, you would not have found in me this prominence in Torah.
suggested_refs: The Roman-era hot springs of Hamat Tiberias
sources: Later Zoharic tradition inverts the relation and makes Pinchas his father-in-law; flagged, not resolved

stops.name: Tiberias, the lupines over the graves
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Jerusalem Talmud; no year given
stops.campa: Herod Antipas built his city over a burial ground, and priests have not been able to enter it since without contracting corpse impurity. Shimon walks the streets scattering crushed lupines, and wherever a seed refuses to root he marks a grave beneath the paving, until the hidden cemetery is charted and the city opens. An elder scoffs that ben Yochai has purified a graveyard. He turns his eyes on the man and the man dies. Then he meets Yehuda ben Gerim in the street, and looks at him, and turns him into a heap of bones.
stops.quote: Since a miracle transpired for me, I will go and repair something for the sake of others in gratitude for God's kindness.
suggested_refs: The unmarked graves of Herodian Tiberias, charted by lupine

stops.name: Usha, the assembly he may or may not have joined
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Encyclopaedia Judaica records both that he took part in the Usha assembly and that he did not
stops.campa: The persecution eases and the surviving sages regather at Usha to rebuild a Sanhedrin out of what is left of one. He had been sentenced to death by Rome within living memory, and ordained in open country by a teacher the soldiers killed on the spot for performing it. Whether he then sat in the reconstituted assembly, the standard encyclopedia declines to say. It inherited two traditions, one that he took part and one that he did not, and printed both without choosing.
suggested_refs: The Usha assembly and its two contradictory traditions about his attendance
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Simeon bar Yohai', via Encyclopedia.com

segments.name: The Rulings and the Road to Rome

stops.name: Rome, the demon and the torn letter
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the Talmud gives the mission without a year
stops.campa: Three decrees stand against the Jews and he is sent to the capital to have them lifted. A demon called Ben Temalion meets him on the road and offers to go ahead: he will enter the emperor's daughter, and when Shimon arrives and orders him out, the court will be grateful. It happens that way. The girl calls out, the spirit leaves her, and the emperor opens his treasury and tells the sage to take whatever he wants. He goes through the room, finds the letter with the decrees in it, and tears it. Me'ilah 17b names nothing in the city, not a street and not a building. It says Rome.
suggested_refs: The imperial treasury of Me'ilah 17b, unlocated in the text

stops.name: Sidon, the feast of the separation
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: A couple come to him from Sidon: ten years married, no child, and the law says the husband must divorce and try again. He tells them to part the way they came together, with a feast. At the feast she fills her husband's cup until he sleeps, and has her servants carry him to her father's house; when he wakes and asks what this is, she says she was told to take home from his house whatever she valued most, and there was nothing there she valued more. Shimon prays over the two of them and they conceive.
suggested_refs: The Sidon couple of Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 22:2

stops.name: Meron, the wish for two mouths
stops.date_confidence: attested saying, unlocated: the Yerushalmi names no place, and Meron is where his school is remembered
stops.campa: He wishes aloud for two mouths: one kept occupied with Torah without a pause in it, one for everything else a body has to say in a day. Then he takes the wish back, and the reason he gives is not that there is too little time. With one mouth, he says, the world can barely stand, because of what men denounce each other with; give a man two and how much worse. The sentence that condemned him was carried out of a room by somebody who had been sitting beside him.
suggested_refs: Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:2, the retraction of the wish

stops.name: Meron, the plowing season, against Rabbi Yishmael
stops.date_confidence: attested saying, unlocated: Berakhot 35b names no place
stops.campa: Rabbi Yishmael reads the verse as permission to carry Torah alongside a trade, in the way of the world. Shimon will not have it: a man who plows in plowing season and sows in sowing season and reaps in reaping season is busy the whole year, and what becomes of Torah then. The Talmud lets the argument stand and then adds a note of its own on how the two ways turned out in practice: many followed Rabbi Yishmael and succeeded, and many followed Rabbi Shimon and did not.
stops.quote: Is it possible that a person plows in the plowing season and sows in the sowing season and harvests in the harvest season... and is constantly busy; what will become of Torah? Rather, one must dedicate himself exclusively to Torah at the expense of other endeavors.
suggested_refs: Abaye's summary at Berakhot 35b on how the two approaches turned out

stops.name: Meron, the fourth crown
stops.date_confidence: attested saying, undated
stops.campa: The Mishnah keeps his ruling on the crowns: three are named and ranked, Torah, priesthood, kingship, and then a fourth is set over all three, one that nobody is born into and no assembly confers. He is a man who was sentenced to death in living memory and ordained in a field by a teacher killed on the spot for doing it. The priesthood is not his by descent. The kingship, in that province and that century, is nobody's at all. The crown he sets over the other three is the crown of a good name.
stops.quote: There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.
suggested_refs: Pirkei Avot 4:13

stops.name: Meron, two Sabbaths
stops.date_confidence: attested saying, undated
stops.campa: He teaches that if Israel kept two Sabbaths properly, one directly after the other, they would be redeemed at once. Not a generation of righteousness, not a war, not a king riding in. Two days, kept as they are written. It is the shortest road to redemption anyone in the tradition proposes, and it is proposed by a man who spent thirteen years underground because Rome wanted him dead, and who came out of the ground setting fields alight with his eyes. Shabbat 118b keeps the saying in his name.
suggested_refs: Shabbat 118b

stops.name: Meron, absolving the world
stops.date_confidence: attested saying, undated
stops.campa: Hizkiya says that Rabbi Yirmeya said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai that he could absolve the whole world from judgment for every sin committed from the day he was created until now, and that with his son beside him, from the day the world was created. In the same passage he says he has seen the men of the highest rank and they are few: if there are a thousand, he and his son are among them; if a hundred, the same; if two, they are he and his son.
stops.quote: I am able to absolve the entire world from judgment for sins committed from the day I was created until now.
suggested_refs: The benei aliyah saying at Sukkah 45b

stops.name: Kfar Bar'am, the facade among the olives
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: local piety, with no inscription and no textual link
stops.campa: The best preserved synagogue ruin in the Upper Galilee stands here among olive terraces near the Lebanese border. No inscription on it carries his name, and no Talmudic passage ties the building to his school; what ties them is the habit these villages have of crediting their good stone to the merit of his disciples, and Kfar Bar'am's is the stone most worth crediting. The facade is still standing to its full height, its doorways open on the terraces and on nothing else.
suggested_refs: The standing south facade of the Kfar Bar'am synagogue
sources: Local Galilean pilgrimage tradition, not attested in Talmudic sources

stops.name: Meron, the boy who will redact the Mishnah
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the biographical tradition places his school here, and later sources name a Galilean Tekoa that some medieval geographers equate with Meron
stops.campa: He settles in the fold of hills under the mountain that will carry his name, and teaches. Among the students is Judah HaNasi, who will redact the Mishnah in which Shimon's own rulings stand among the most frequently cited of any sage's. Later sources put the school at a Galilean Tekoa instead, a place medieval geographers sometimes equate with Meron and sometimes hold separate, and which no excavation has ever fixed. Of whatever house or study hall he kept here, nothing above ground survives.
suggested_refs: The halakhic midrash collections Sifre and Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon, credited to his school by later tradition and unconfirmed by critical scholarship
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Simeon bar Yohai', via Encyclopedia.com
Medieval geographic tradition on Tekoa of the Galilee

stops.name: Meron, the Great Assembly in the valley
stops.date_confidence: literary setting: the Idra Rabba is a thirteenth-century Kabbalistic composition staged at Meron, not a datable event
stops.campa: In the Zohar's staging he calls ten companions into a valley below the village and opens the deepest strata of the teaching, the configurations of the divine face, matters not said aloud since Sinai. Three of the ten do not survive the transmission. The scene belongs to Castile in the thirteenth century and is set here, at the house of the man whose name it is written in. The valley the text describes has never been matched to any spot on this hillside.
suggested_refs: The Idra Rabba, staged in a valley below Meron

stops.name: Meron, the Small Assembly
stops.date_confidence: literary setting: the Idra Zuta, a thirteenth-century composition, not a datable event
stops.campa: The companions are gathered a last time, and in the Zohar's account the house fills with fire and nobody can look at him directly while he speaks. He dies mid-word, the sentence unfinished, the teaching still coming out of him. This is medieval Kabbalah narrating a second-century deathbed it was not present at, in the register of an eyewitness. Around that bed the text puts light and speech where the biographical sources put nothing whatever: no year, no illness, no season, no room.
suggested_refs: The Idra Zuta, the deathbed assembly of the Zohar

stops.name: Meron, the day kept as a completion
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no Talmudic or midrashic source gives a year, and the date is placement by generation
stops.campa: He dies at Meron in old age. The midrashic sources describe the day of his death as one the community treats with joy rather than mourning, because he asked that it be marked as a completion and not as a loss. What those sources preserve is the observance. The death itself they leave bare: no source gives a year, and none gives the manner of it. The death is placed only by where it sits in his generation, somewhere in the middle or the later part of the second century.
suggested_refs: The traditional burial cave at Meron

stops.name: Meron, the son brought back
stops.date_confidence: attested in Pesikta de-Rav Kahana; undated
stops.campa: Elazar dies and is buried at Gush Halav, the olive town where his father's household is remembered, and not beside his father. Why the two were separated the text does not explain, and it does not say who chose the ground. Afterward the people of Meron petition for the bones. They are carried up the hill and laid with Shimon's, putting back into one grave a father and son who had shared a cave, a sand floor, and thirteen years of one unbroken conversation. The two names have been on the tomb together ever since.
suggested_refs: The joint tomb of Shimon and Elazar at Meron

stops.name: Meron, the first document that names the grave
stops.date_confidence: attested: the itinerary is dated to the first third of the thirteenth century
stops.campa: The traveller Jacob ben Netanel ha-Kohen writes down that the tombs of Shimon bar Yochai and his son are at Meron, and his itinerary is the earliest surviving document to say so, roughly eleven hundred years after the death it locates. Archaeology finds Mishnaic-period rock-cut burials on the site and nothing that attributes any of them to anyone; one excavator states flatly that no archaeological evidence exists for the identification. A medieval tradition once gave the same prominent grave to Hillel.
suggested_refs: Jacob ben Netanel ha-Kohen's thirteenth-century travelogue
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'
Prof. Mordechai Aviam, quoted in the Jerusalem Post, 'Is Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai really buried at Meron? It's complicated'

stops.name: Meron, the book that says it was written here
stops.date_confidence: attested for the circulation date; the authorship is the standing contradiction of this file
stops.campa: A book begins circulating in Castile, in Aramaic, presenting itself as the record of what he taught his companions in the Galilee, much of it out of the cave years. Medieval Kabbalah takes the framing literally and reads it as his. Gershom Scholem's philology takes it apart: the Aramaic is artificial, the grammar Spanish underneath, the geography of the Land of Israel wrong in ways no Galilean could manage, and the author is Moses de Leon of Castile. Scholem published that argument in 1926. The traditional attribution has not been withdrawn.
suggested_refs: The Cremona and Mantua first printings of the Zohar, both 1558
The Zohar: Pritzker Edition, twelve volumes, Stanford University Press, 2004-2017
Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's Kabbalistic theses of 1486, built on Latin translations of the Zohar
Arthur Edward Waite, The Holy Kabbalah (London, 1929)
sources: Gershom Scholem, 'Is Moses de Leon the Author of the Zohar?' (1926)
Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)
Traditional Kabbalistic attribution, per the Schechter Institute treatise on the Meron hillula

stops.name: Meron, the Musta'arabi caretakers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period before 1492; no precise year
stops.campa: Before the refugees of the Spanish expulsion reach the Galilee, the site is kept by Musta'arabi Jews, Arabic-speaking, indigenous, long in place. They are the ones who maintain the grave through the centuries in which it is a local matter and not a national one, and they are recorded as managing it when the newcomers arrive. After 1492 the Sephardim come up the hill with the Zohar in their baggage. Who was left holding the keys a generation later is not something the record says.
suggested_refs: The Musta'arabi communities of the Galilee before 1492
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'

stops.name: Meron, the eighteenth of Iyar
stops.date_confidence: attested: Isaac Luria is the first writer known to state that the death fell on Lag BaOmer
stops.campa: The kabbalists of Safed take him for their patron and the Zohar for their book, and Isaac Luria, the Ari, is the first writer known to state outright that he died on Lag BaOmer, the thirty-third day of the Omer count. Out of that sentence the festival grows: a bonfire lit after dark on the roof of the tomb, singing, dancing, and the first haircut of three-year-old boys, brought up the mountain to be shorn beside the grave. None of it reaches back to the second century.
suggested_refs: The Lag BaOmer bonfire on the roof of the tomb
sources: Schechter Institute, 'A Historical Treatise on the Lag B'Omer Celebration at Mt. Meron'
Chabad.org, 'Meron - Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'
Wikipedia, 'Hillula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'

stops.name: Meron, Galante's mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sources say only that Abraham ben Mordecai Galante is said to have built it
stops.campa: Abraham ben Mordecai Galante of Safed is said to have raised a mausoleum over the grave. Said to have: the hedge belongs to the sources, and it is not worth smoothing away. One strand of writing turns this sixteenth-century structure into the building pilgrims walk through today, merely renovated later. The better-sourced account has it superseded outright by a nineteenth-century construction. The two accounts cannot both be describing the same stones. Which of them the standing walls belong to is left open.
suggested_refs: The disputed fabric of the tomb building at Meron
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'
Grokipedia and galilandgolan.com, carrying the contradicting sixteenth-century-building claim; named here as the weak sourcing it is

stops.name: Meron, the consular agent buys the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Shmuel Abu, a French consular agent who had come to Safed from Algeria, buys the land around the tomb. For six hundred years the grave has been in the keeping of whoever lived nearest to it and cared for it. Now it is a property with a deed behind it and a foreign consulate standing behind the deed, in a century when consular protection is how anything in Ottoman Palestine is held onto at all. The purchase is dated 1817. What Abu put up on the ground came three decades later.
suggested_refs: The Abu family holdings around the Meron tomb
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'

stops.name: Meron, the building that stands
stops.date_confidence: attested for the construction; the sources give mid-century rather than a year
stops.campa: Abu builds the tomb structure that is substantially the one standing now: courtyards, separate chambers for men and for women, the pale domes visible from the road below, and a roof flat enough to build a fire on. Thirty years later, in 1881, the surveyors of Western Palestine walk up, look at it, and write it down as apparently a modern building. That is what it is. The stonework visitors touch at the most venerated grave in the Galilee was laid in the eighteen-fifties.
suggested_refs: The Survey of Western Palestine's description of the tomb, 1881
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'

stops.name: Meron, the balcony
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A balcony gives way during the Lag BaOmer gathering and eleven people are killed out of some ten thousand present. The crowd on the mountain has by now outgrown every structure built to hold it, and the arrangement governing the site is not really a governing arrangement: no single body holds the day, the buildings, and the safety of the people standing on them. It is the first time the festival kills anybody. The dead are counted and the collapse is written down. The following year the bonfire is lit on the roof at the usual hour.

stops.name: Peki'in, the carob they show you
stops.date_confidence: the synagogue restoration is dated 1955; the pilgrimage to the cave above the village is continuous and undated
stops.campa: The cave above the village keeps a smaller traffic than the tomb, visited by people retracing the thirteen years rather than the death. A large old carob stands beside it and is shown as the tree, or as the tree's descendant. Peki'in held one of the oldest continuously inhabited Jewish communities in the Galilee until the middle of the twentieth century, and its synagogue was restored in 1955 at President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi's request; two stones inside are said locally to have been carried there from the ruins of the Second Temple.
suggested_refs: The Peki'in synagogue and its two traditionally Temple-derived stones
sources: showcaves.com, 'Cave of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai'

stops.name: Meron, the competition
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eight years after statehood a design competition is held for the renovation of the complex, and the architect Yosef Shenberger wins it. The layout is formalized for a pilgrimage that now arrives by bus and in numbers no medieval traveller would recognize. Ownership of the site is contested between Sephardic and Ashkenazic religious trusts before the competition is announced and after it is decided. The competition settles the buildings. It does not touch the question of who owns them.

stops.name: Meron, the night of the crush
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the night of Lag BaOmer roughly a hundred thousand people are on the mountain, and the crowd funnels into a narrow, steep stairway slick with spilled drink. Forty-five men and boys are crushed to death and about a hundred and fifty are injured, the deadliest civil disaster in the country's history. The state commission reports in 2024 and assigns personal responsibility to the prime minister, to police commanders, and to local officials, citing negligence, absent governance, and years in which construction-safety law was simply not enforced on the site.
